academicTalks.transcript: Today I want to talk about something sociologists call social networks, which are simply the patterns of connection between people. In one study, researchers looked at how students in a large course formed study groups. They found that most groups came together within the first two or three weeks of the semester, often starting from just a few classmates sitting near each other. What's interesting is how information spread through these groups. Sociologists distinguish between strong ties, like close friends, and weak ties, casual acquaintances you don't know well. It turned out that weak ties, not strong ones, were responsible for spreading most academic tips—things like which sections of the textbook to focus on, or how a professor tends to write exam questions. To track this, the researchers surveyed students every few weeks, mapping who talked to whom across the whole semester. Students who joined a study network early on reported missing far fewer assignment deadlines than students who joined later or never joined at all. The researchers suggest that early connection, even a weak one, matters more than we usually assume.

A weak tie is an acquaintance you've met exclusively through a mutual online platform or social media application
A weak tie exists only between people who share the same academic major

questions.explanationZh: 講者定義弱連結為不熟識的普通熟人（casual acquaintance you don't know well），與親密朋友的強連結相對；其餘選項提到限定於網路平台認識、畢業後才形成、僅限同科系，原文均未提及。

academicTalks.transcript: Let's look at how city governments actually decide where public money goes. Most city budgets include a formal public comment period, a stretch of time when residents can submit feedback before the city council votes on the final numbers. This period typically runs about three weeks, giving people enough time to review the proposal and respond. During that window, cities often run resident surveys asking which services matter most—things like road repair, park maintenance, or public transit. In many cases, spending priorities actually shift after these surveys come in; a city might move money from one department to another based on what residents say they value most. Because budget documents can run hundreds of pages and use a lot of technical language, many cities now publish a plain-language summary alongside the full document. This summary highlights the major changes and new spending in terms an average resident can understand without needing a background in public finance. By the end of the comment period, the council has usually adjusted its proposal at least somewhat based on what it heard.

academicTalks.transcript: How does a touchscreen actually know where your finger is? Most modern screens use what's called capacitive sensing. Underneath the glass is a grid of electrodes that each hold a small electrical charge. Your fingertip, because it naturally conducts a little electricity, disturbs that charge slightly wherever it touches the screen. Older resistive screens, by contrast, worked by physically pressing two layers together, which required more pressure and reacted more slowly. Capacitive sensors respond much faster because they don't need physical pressure at all—just the tiny charge change from your finger nearby. Of course, sensing a charge change isn't the same as knowing you tapped a button. That's where software comes in. The device constantly reads the raw sensor data and converts those charge patterns into a specific screen location, which the software then interprets as a tap, swipe, or drag. One challenge engineers face is that a giant tablet screen and a small phone screen need different sensitivity settings—too sensitive, and stray touches register; too weak, and real taps get missed. So each device size is calibrated individually before it ships.

academicTalks.transcript: Have you ever noticed you get hungry around the same time every day, even before you look at a clock? That's not just habit—it's partly biology. Your body produces a hunger hormone whose levels naturally rise before a typical mealtime and fall again after you eat. Researchers have found that eating at consistent times each day actually reinforces this daily rhythm. The more regularly you eat at the same hours, the more predictably that hormone rises and falls around those times, almost like your body learns the schedule. But what happens if you skip a meal? Studies show that hunger signals don't just disappear—they shift. If you miss lunch, for example, the hormone spike that would normally happen around midday gets delayed, and you may feel a stronger pull toward the next meal instead. The good news is that this shifted pattern doesn't last. Once you go back to eating at your usual times, the daily rhythm resets within a few days, returning to its original schedule. So an occasional skipped meal doesn't permanently disrupt your body's sense of timing.

questions.stem: What is this talk mainly about?

options.text: How exercise changes hunger hormone levels
How different foods affect digestion speed
Why some people never feel hungry
How the body's hunger signals follow a daily rhythm

questions.explanationZh: 整篇主旨在說明飢餓訊號如何依循每日規律變化（daily rhythm），並非討論消化速度、完全不感飢餓或運動的影響。
